title: The bystander
hookLine: people help less when others are around, though the well-known New York case was reported inaccurately (Latané and Darley)

cards: Somebody should do something. That thought turns up at a crash on the highway, on a train when someone sways and sits down hard, in a meeting where a question hangs in the air. The word doing the work is somebody.
Not me, not you. Somebody. Two psychologists, Bibb Latané and John Darley, wanted to see what happens to that somebody as a room fills up with other people.
So they sat people down with a questionnaire, and then piped smoke in through a vent in the wall.

teach.b: First, the smoke room. As the smoke drifted in and began to haze the air, some people sat alone, and some sat with two actors told to stay calm and ignore it. People alone usually got up and reported it.
People with the calm actors mostly didn't. They waved the smoke away, kept writing, and later explained that it probably wasn't dangerous. Second, why.
The researchers pointed to two forces.

teach.h: READING THE ROOM, SPREADING IT THIN.
teach.b: One is reading the room: if nobody else looks worried, maybe it's fine. The other is spreading responsibility thin: with others present, each person feels less like it's up to them.
It's sometimes called the bystander effect. Third, an honest correction. This research is often told alongside a murder in New York, reported in a newspaper as neighbors watching and doing nothing.
Later reporting found that account badly overstated. Few people saw much, some did call, and at least one neighbor went to her.
The smoke room happened as described; the story told alongside it was not accurate. Fourth, an old answer.
The Jewish teacher Hillel, in Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, says in effect: in a place where no one is acting like a decent human being, try to be one.
Beside the smoke room, it sounds like advice for exactly that moment. When everyone is waiting for someone, decide that someone is you.

how: First-aid and safety trainings often teach people to point at one specific person and ask them to call for help, so responsibility isn't spread thin; in Jewish teaching, Pirkei Avot records Hillel urging a person to act humanely where no one else does.

o: a person who chooses to harm others in a crowd
one of many who each wait for someone else to help
a witness called to testify about what they saw

games.q: inside the smoke room: tap the pairs.
p: usually got up and reported it
nobody looks worried, so maybe it's fine
where no one acts humanely, be the one

s: the well-known New York murder story was reported accurately
later reporting found it was badly overstated; some neighbors called, and at least one went to her.
people alone in the smoke room usually reported the smoke
it was the people sitting with calm actors who mostly stayed put.
the bystander effect means people don't care
the researchers pointed to reading the room and spreading responsibility thin, not to cold hearts.

games.q: smoke is pouring in. two people at your table keep writing calmly. what did most people in that seat do?
o: left the building without a word.
games.why: with two calm actors beside them, most people stayed put and told themselves it was probably fine.

practice: Picture a moment when you'll be one of many: a meeting where a question hangs unanswered, a sidewalk where someone drops their groceries, a group chat where a friend's sad message gets no reply.
See yourself moving first, not dramatically, just first, and hold the one most likely to happen today as you rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: The bystander. With others around, people often help less: they read the room and spread responsibility thin, so someone has to go first. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: be the one. Somebody, it turns out, can be anybody in the room. Thirteen-ten, in the books.
